questions.statement: ___ the tickets online, you avoid the long queue at the counter.
questions.context: A present participle phrase at the start of a sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! An active action happening at the same time as the main verb takes the present participle.
A past participle would show the booking as complete before the main verb, and both actions are simultaneous.
An infinitive would express purpose, and the sentence is describing two simultaneous actions.
A perfect participle would put the booking first, which reverses the order of the two events.

questions.explanation:
A present participle phrase shows an action happening at the same time as the main verb. Having plus a past participle is the form for an earlier action.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the report, she went home early.
questions.context: A perfect participle phrase, where the first action is earlier.

options.feedback: Correct! Having plus a past participle shows that finishing came before going home.
The present participle would place the two actions at the same time, and going home clearly came second.
A past participle without having would be a reduced passive relative clause, which is a different structure.
An infinitive expresses purpose and would need a subject of its own to work here.

questions.explanation:
The order of the two events decides the participle. Simultaneous actions take the present participle, and an action completed first takes having plus the past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ by the storm, the old tree fell across the road.
questions.context: A passive participle phrase, where the subject receives the action.

options.feedback: Correct! A past participle with by forms a reduced passive relative clause describing the tree.
The -ing form would make the tree the agent of the damaging, which is not the meaning.
A perfect participle would make the tree the agent of the action rather than the patient.
An infinitive cannot begin a participle phrase in this position.

questions.explanation:
A past participle with a by phrase reduces a passive relative clause. Damaged by the storm tells us what happened to the tree without repeating the relative pronoun.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He was ___ in the middle of the sentence when the phone rang.
questions.context: The two participles of the verb break, which are both irregular.

options.feedback: Correct! The present participle of break is breaking, with the internal e preserved.
Break is irregular and has no -ed form in the present participle.
Broke is the past simple and cannot follow the auxiliary was as a participle.
Broken is the past participle and would need have or been rather than was.

questions.explanation:
Break keeps the e in the present participle, as do write, take, drive and come. The internal vowel rule is the reason those participles look irregular.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The train, ___ at 6 a.m., arrives before noon.
questions.context: A participle phrase that follows the subject, which changes the emphasis.

options.feedback: Correct! A present participle after the subject adds descriptive information about the train's schedule.
A past participle would describe the train as the one that left, and it has not left yet.
A perfect participle would place the departure before the arrival, which is not the schedule.
An infinitive after the subject would make the sentence ungrammatical in this position.

questions.explanation:
A participle phrase can stand after the subject as well as before it. Placing it after the subject keeps the main subject nearer the beginning of the sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The results ___ by the committee at three o'clock will be posted online.
questions.context: A participle phrase in a passive sentence, reduced.

options.feedback: Correct! A past participle reduces a passive relative clause, so the results are what was approved.
A reduced clause drops the relative pronoun, and the full form would be results that were approved.
A reduced clause has no auxiliary, because the main verb will be posted already carries the tense.
The -ing form would make the results the agent of the approving, which is not what happens.

questions.explanation:
The results approved is a reduced relative clause. The committee did the approving, and the results received it, so the passive participle is required.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The letter ___ by the secretary and ___ by the director yesterday.
questions.context: Two participles with different auxiliaries in the same sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! Two past passive actions need the auxiliary was twice, and yesterday makes the past tense certain.
A present passive would place both actions now, and yesterday is in the past.
A present perfect would leave the actions inside the present period, and yesterday closes them.
Being belongs to continuous passives, and the actions are not described as running in parallel.

questions.explanation:
Each participle phrase carries its own auxiliary. When two of them share the same tense, the auxiliary has to be written out for each one.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He has been ___ in the same job for fifteen years.
questions.context: A present participle used for an action happening over a long period.

options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect continuous uses have plus been plus the present participle.
A past participle with have been is not a valid form, because been already carries the auxiliary.
An infinitive cannot follow the auxiliary been in a continuous structure.
The in belongs with the preposition in the following clause, not with the participle itself.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect continuous is have plus been plus -ing. The past participle has no place in that structure because the auxiliary is already there.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ in the rain, we had to stop the match.
questions.context: A participle phrase expressing the reason for an action.

options.feedback: Correct! A present participle phrase at the start of a sentence can express the cause of the main clause.
A past participle would describe the match as the one getting wet, but the players are in the rain.
An infinitive phrase cannot begin a sentence as a participle clause.
A perfect participle would suggest the two are in a fixed order, and here they happen together.

questions.explanation:
A participle phrase at the start of a sentence can supply the reason, the condition or the time. Its logical relationship to the main clause comes from the situation, not from a conjunction.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She is ___ a cup of tea and reading the newspaper.
questions.context: A participle of a verb that ends in an e.

options.feedback: Correct! Drink keeps the e in the present participle, so the form is drinking.
Drink is irregular and has no -ed form in the present participle.
Drank is the past simple and cannot follow the auxiliary is as a participle.
Drunk is the past participle and would need have or been rather than is.

questions.explanation:
Verbs ending in a silent e keep that e before -ing. Drink becomes drinking, and the same rule applies to write, take, make and come.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The woman ___ at the desk is the new principal.
questions.context: A participle phrase describing a person, in a reduced relative clause.

options.feedback: Correct! An active reduced relative clause takes the present participle, and the woman is the one working.
A reduced clause has no auxiliary, because the main verb of the sentence already carries the tense.
A past participle would describe a passive clause, and the woman is working rather than being worked.
A reduced clause drops the relative pronoun, so that cannot stay in front of the participle.

questions.explanation:
An active reduced clause uses the -ing form and a passive one uses the past participle. Neither keeps the relative pronoun or the auxiliary.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She has been ___ in the hospital for a week.
questions.context: A participle in a sentence about a duration.

options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect continuous is have plus been plus the present participle.
A base form cannot follow the auxiliary been in a continuous structure.
A past participle would give have been recovered, which describes something done to her.
An infinitive has no place between been and the main verb of the sentence.

questions.explanation:
For plus a duration with have been plus -ing is the present perfect continuous. The -ing form is compulsory in that structure.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The film ___ by a small studio was a surprise success.
questions.context: The past participle of a verb ending in a consonant plus y.

options.feedback: Correct! Make is irregular and its past participle is made, with no change to the stem.
Maked is not a form of make, which is irregular in the past.
The -ing form would reduce an active clause, and the film was the thing produced rather than the producer.
Did cannot precede a past participle, because the auxiliary and the participle are alternatives.

questions.explanation:
Irregular participles must be learned rather than worked out. Make, wrote and done are the ones most often confused with a regular -ed form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the interview, the candidate left the building.
questions.context: A participle phrase in a sentence with two past actions.

options.feedback: Correct! Having plus a past participle shows the interview finished before the leaving.
A present participle after after would show the two actions at the same time, which is not what happened.
Being would make the candidate the agent of the taking, and after being taken is not a natural sequence here.
An infinitive cannot open a participle clause after a preposition in this structure.

questions.explanation:
After having plus a past participle is a common way of showing sequence. After plus a present participle would suggest the two actions overlap instead.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The bridge, ___ in 1960, is still in daily use.
questions.context: A passive participle with a by phrase in the middle of a sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! A past participle with a by phrase reduces a passive relative clause.
The -ing form would make the bridge the agent of the building, which is not the case.
A reduced clause has no auxiliary, because the main verb of the sentence already carries the tense.
A reduced clause drops the relative pronoun, and the full form would be which was built.

questions.explanation:
A reduced passive clause is a past participle plus an optional by phrase. It compresses a whole relative clause into a single phrase.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ tomorrow morning, the new bus service will begin operating.
questions.context: A participle phrase in a future sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! A present participle can be used with a future reference, and the two actions are simultaneous in the future.
A past participle would suggest the start is already complete, and the service has not begun.
A perfect participle would place the start before the service begins, and the moment the question refers to has not arrived.
An infinitive phrase cannot open a participle clause in this position.

questions.explanation:
Participle phrases are not tied to the present tense. A present participle can describe an action that is simultaneous with a future main verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ from the airport, they went straight to the hotel.
questions.context: A participle phrase where the action is clearly earlier than the main verb.

options.feedback: Correct! The present participle works here because both actions belong to the same moment of the story.
A perfect participle would emphasise the order strictly, and here the two actions are reported together.
A bare past participle would be a reduced passive clause, and they are the ones arriving rather than being arrived.
An infinitive cannot open a participle clause.

questions.explanation:
Arriving and having arriving are both possible, and the choice depends on how strictly the order is being emphasised. With a short clause like this, the present participle reads more naturally.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Not ___ the tickets in advance, they had to queue for hours.
questions.context: A participle phrase in a negative sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! Not plus having plus a past participle gives a negative perfect participle phrase.
A base form cannot follow not in a participle phrase.
A past participle after not would need having in front of it to form a perfect participle.
An infinitive has no place in a negative participle phrase.

questions.explanation:
A negative participle phrase is formed by putting not in front of the whole phrase. Not having bought and not buying are both available, with different shades of meaning.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the results, will the team travel to the final?
questions.context: A participle phrase in a question.

options.feedback: Correct! A perfect participle phrase can open a question and shows the results were examined first.
See is irregular and its past participle is seen, not saw.
A present participle would place the two actions at the same moment, and the results come first.
A bare past participle would be a reduced passive clause, and the team is the one seeing the results.

questions.explanation:
Participle phrases are not restricted to declarative sentences. They can open questions as well, and the -ing or having choice follows the same order rule.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the deadline, she submitted the work just in time.
questions.context: A participle phrase in a sentence with a past perfect.

options.feedback: Correct! A present participle phrase can accompany a past perfect main clause without any conflict of tense.
A past participle after a past perfect would describe her as being met, and she is the one meeting the deadline.
A perfect participle would add a third layer of past reference, and the sentence does not need it.
An infinitive cannot open a participle clause.

questions.explanation: A participle phrase is independent of the main clause tense. A present participle can sit in front of a past perfect just as easily as in front of a present simple.
questions.subject: ingles
